results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 96 aligned units' outline summaries match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, in spec order; the three callouts carry the hook/thesis per the spec's placement and match no paragraph. The outline's extra ideas in p05, p28, p60 and p82 are each named in that paragraph's own spec entry (controlling idea or evidence).
The reverse outline, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the spec's introduction, fourteen sections and conclusion (see reverse_outline_matches_spec).

Outliner marked four units with two ideas; each second idea is part of the spec paragraph's declared content: p05's Tool 11 sentence instances 'linked from the tools that depend on them'; p28's vertical mappings are listed in p28's evidence (the example exercising the table's mapping rule); p60's legal/engineering review is in its controlling idea; p82's public cases are its declared evidence for 'the constraints row binds'. (p05's sentence is judged separately under flow_is_followable for placement and accuracy.)

Every unit traces to T1 (lookup, connections), T2 (each tool's purpose/when/template/example/mistakes/chapter), T3 (removal, ownership and date fields; incident replays in p42, p49, p63, p71, p78) or T4 (maintained data, identifiers, conclusion habits).

Each table and figure is introduced and read: lookup table by p04, Figure 1 by p06 and its caption, each template by its one-line lead, each Veldmark example by the analysis paragraph that follows (p11, p18, p28, p35, p42, p49, p56, p63, p71, p78, p85, p92); the CMA and Kleinanzeigen sources in p82 are each tied to what they show (constraints bind; a brand migration takes years of redirects).

Every boundary expresses its declared relationship: elaboration (p02 'Three conventions run through all twelve'), sequence (p03, 'Use it when' openers, the Tool 3 table labels), example ('Veldmark example'), cause_effect (p11 'The verdict follows from the scores', p42, p71, p78), emphasis (p49 'The removal row is the one...', p63, p85 'The two columns are the point of the card'), contrast ('Common mistakes', p05 'not repeated here'), additional_support (p18, p69, p92, 'Learn more'), conclusion_summary (p95).

results.draft_locus: Find the Template for the Question on Your Desk ¶2
results.quote: Tool 11's data row links the qualified-contact definition in [[data-platform]] directly.
results.finding: flowA A17: the sentence refers to a row of a tool the reader has not met and feels out of place right after the lookup table. It is also inaccurate: Tool 11's Data row (Hearthly.es column) links [[data-platform]] for 'governed data products under group contracts' and says nothing about a qualified-contact definition. Drop the sentence or replace it with an accurate, general statement that the tools link these records where a field depends on them.

results.draft_locus: How the Records Connect ¶1 (and the Figure 1 caption)
results.quote: Nearly every operational record rests on the SLA card (Tool 6) and the listing event specification (Tool 10), so earlier tools refer forward to them.
results.finding: flowA A16: the Figure 1 caption orders the records by dependency (Tools 1-2 feed decisions in Tools 11-12, which produce Tools 3-4 and 5/10), while the sections follow part order with Tools 11 and 12 last; the paragraph explains only the forward references to Tools 6 and 10, so the reader wondered why the decision tools come at the end. The spec's order is sound and justified; one clause saying the tools follow the part order, not the diagram's flow, would remove the stumble.

results.quote: The table's "Alertable: No" for Sold is the rule the evening alert digest broke: assembled at 17:30, before the sale, it was sent the next morning without a re-check (Tool 6 picks up that digest).
results.finding: flowB B8: the digest failure is packed into the bike's sale timeline (14:02 reserved, 18:10 sold, 18:11 removed, then a digest assembled at 17:30 and sent next morning) and the paragraph ends on unrelated vertical mappings; the reader re-read to separate the sale and digest timelines. flowA A8 reports the same passage as an abrupt jump to 'the evening alert digest'. The names (Femke, Safe Deal) are known to the declared audience; the problem is the interleaved timelines. The spec's content for p28 is fine; the prose should mark the shift to the digest (and its time relative to the sale) more clearly.

results.quote: Without it, analytics recorded Femke's sale as "expired"
results.finding: flowA A9 only: the past tense does not show that this was the state before the outcome field existed; reader re-read. Minor.

Terms the flow readers flagged as unexplained are in the spec's audience.already_knows: the brands, Femke, Safe Deal, the Essen Golf, Yardstick, Common Ground, Casavista, Veldmark ID, the neutrality decision and the architecture advice forum are introduced in meet-veldmark; Ghost Inventory, Forced Fit, Search as System of Record and the attribute junkyard in where-listing-systems-go-wrong; effect projector, consumer registry and Tenancy model v1 come from the owning chapters (products-and-entitlements, event-driven-listings, multi-country-platforms) the audience knows or opens from each tool. Neither does_not_know item is a term; both are given (lookup table; ownership/removal/date fields in p01 and the KEY POINTS).
Opens with a direct statement ('These are working templates for a group of listing marketplaces'), states the thesis, conventions and roadmap; no throat-clearing, dictionary opening or vague promise.

The conclusion is not a section-by-section recap or a new topic: it synthesizes why the fields exist (incidents), gives three habits as a course of action, then hands off to the glossary and bibliography as specified.

'Each template leaves evidence someone else can check only while it stays true, above all in the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates' plus 'Let incidents add fields' (38,400 cars, 214 digests, €212,000, three days to cross a border) synthesize the examples; the so-what is the course of action: review on a calendar, add a field when a post-incident review finds a gap, remove fields nobody reads.
Calls back to p01's 'leaves evidence someone else can check' and 'the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates', now explained by the incidents the examples replay.

The introduction-only reader predicted the page in order: lookup table, diagram of citations, twelve tools in part order each with purpose/when/template/Veldmark example/three mistakes/chapter, keeping templates true, sources, then glossary and bibliography; this matches the roadmap and the sections.

AC-2 reader (opening only) gave all three expected answers: twelve working templates for the records Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep, each with a Veldmark example, mistakes and chapter; start with the record that changes the decision this week, keep them as maintained data cited by identifier; the fields for ownership, removal behavior and dates are dropped first. Noted, not failing: the reader saw a tension between KEY POINT 1's 'an owner, a stable identifier and a measurable promise' and p01's 'ownership, removal behavior and dates'.

AC-1 reader found all three from the lookup table: (a) Tool 5 feed contract, listing-ingestion, absence_means / mass-change guard; (b) Tool 11 consolidation decision card, platform-consolidation, constraints row and exit path (the exit path is what Common mistakes calls separability, matching the expected 'cost to reverse'); (c) Tool 9 entitlement matrix, products-and-entitlements, failure column and billing basis. The reader noted that rows for Tools 2, 7 and 12 could also claim (b); the table still led it to Tool 11.
